analysis.title: Silicon Just Overtook Oil: Deutsche Warns The "Chip-Dollar" Is Replacing The Petrodollar, And It's Far More Fragile
key_insights: Deutsche Bank FX strategist Mallika Sachdeva argues the petrodollar is being superseded by a chip-dollar. Global trade in semiconductors exceeded trade in oil and gas over the four quarters to Q2 2026, for the first time.

Chip surpluses in Asia ex-China (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, ASEAN) have caught up with Gulf petroleum surpluses, both in the mid-$300 billions on a four-quarter basis. The chip line is rising and the oil line is rolling over.

South Korea's chip trade surplus is close to $250 billion, equal to 100% of its total trade surplus, with chip exports up more than 200% YoY this year. The surplus is recycled abroad entirely through equities.

Foreign sales of Korean equities account for half of Korean capital outflows over the past year and Korean purchases of overseas equities the other half. Korean overseas equity investment has been five times Korean purchases of overseas bonds over two years.
The US is about 50% of global equity market cap but 70% of Korea's overseas equity holdings (IMF CPIS) and more than 90% for Korean retail investors.
Foreign purchases of US equities topped $1 trillion over the past year, more than double the flow into Treasuries. Foreign purchases of US corporate bonds now also exceed Treasuries.

Of the rise in the 12-month sum of foreign US equity purchases between August 2025 and August 2026, Asia contributed about $185 billion and the Caribbean about $125 billion. Europe contributed little.

Chips account for over half of AI data center capex: servers are about 60% of the annualized cost of a 1GW data center (Epoch AI) and chips are 95% of a server rack's value (SIA). Bloomberg Intelligence puts hyperscaler capex commitments near $8 trillion through 2031, which Deutsche says implies about $4 trillion of further chip demand.

US firms capture about 70% of semiconductor profits: design is about 50% of supply chain value with US firms holding 87% of design revenue, near-monopoly in EDA software and about 60% of chip-equipment revenue. Manufacturing, packaging and testing in Asia are about 30%.

China runs a chip deficit despite a manufactured goods surplus above $2 trillion. Under 20% of its net international assets are portfolio investments, against nearly 50% for Korea, Japan and Taiwan, and it favors hard assets and gold.

Deutsche flags circularity: US AI equity flows are funded by Asian chip surpluses that are boosted by US AI demand. If compute demand fails to match supply investment, earnings estimates and chip demand would fall, weakening foreign equity financing of the US on both the push and pull side.

Realized vol on the S&P 500 has recently been three times that of 10Y Treasuries, the Nasdaq's double the S&P's, and the Philly semis index's more than triple. Sachdeva expects US deficit financing's dependence on a more volatile asset class to spill over into currency volatility.

Saravelos (Deutsche) argues about 90% of the $20+ trillion in US equities owned by foreigners is price appreciation ('for every $1 bought, there is $10 to sell'), and that when the equity shock is US-made, the dollar falls with stocks.

The Taiex fell 6.03% in a session, the fifth-largest decline in 10 years per Goldman's Asia desk, on hedge fund selling of TSMC and broad tech shorts. Foreigners sold a net NT$70.2 billion (about $2.13 billion) of Taiwanese stocks. The Kospi fell 4%, Advantest fell 11.1% and Tokyo Electron fell 7.1%.
Taiwan's central bank governor said the bank has intervened in FX more often since October and that TWD moves are tied to local stock moves and foreign outflows, not rate differentials.

Goldman's 2027 Global FX Outlook (Trivedi et al.) expects dollar tailwinds, including surging AI-related investment expectations, to turn into headwinds next year, with KRW and TWD among the outperformers. Goldman says the shift will be gradual.

Zero Hedge's own view: the next leg of the AI unwind is more likely US-made, which would make the dollar part of the trade rather than a hedge. Nvidia reports into congressional scrutiny and a Democratic Congress arrives in January.

market_movers.rationale: Goldman's Asia desk said multiple hedge funds sold TSMC aggressively as the Taiex fell 6.03%.
Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday amid congressional scrutiny and possible tighter US export controls, following recent events at Nvidia.

sector_views.rationale: Chips are the largest line in AI data center capex and 70% of profits go to US firms, but the loop is circular and the Philly semis index realized vol is more than triple the S&P 500's.

earnings_insights: Nvidia is due to report earnings on Tuesday (the day after the Taiex plunge). The note gives no estimates.

risk_factors: Circularity: US AI equity flows funded by Asian chip surpluses that depend on US AI demand.
Weak demand for compute relative to supply investment would cut earnings estimates and chip demand.
Currency volatility spillover from deficit financing relying on a more volatile asset class.
Tighter US export controls and a shift in US political climate.
Concentration risk in Korea, where chips are 100% of the trade surplus.
Retail leverage and momentum chasing in Korea and Japan.
vol_and_positioning: Realized vol on the S&P 500 recently three times that of 10Y Treasuries, Nasdaq double the S&P 500, Philly semis index more than triple.
Zero Hedge's napkin math: the asset underwriting the dollar is roughly ten times as volatile as the one that used to.
Korean retail ('ants') holds more than 90% of its overseas equity exposure in US assets and returned to buying ten days after the summer Kospi rout.
Saravelos: about 90% of foreign-owned US equities' value is price appreciation, so for every $1 bought there is $10 to sell.
Korea's circuit breakers tripped in mid-October on foreign selling of memory names.
geopolitical: Iran war: Deutsche still thinks it is eroding the petrodollar, against a WSJ rebuttal that it was a boon for it.
Possible tighter US export controls on chips, with Washington potentially doubling down after recent events at Nvidia.
Changing political climate in the US, including a Democratic Congress arriving in January.

tension_points.bull_case: Asian chip surpluses are being recycled into US equities, funding US AI investment and supporting the dollar. Foreign purchases of US equities exceed $1 trillion a year.
tension_points.bear_case: The loop is circular and the asset class underwriting the dollar is far more volatile than Treasuries. A reassessment of compute demand would cut chip demand and foreign equity financing of the US together.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Consumer demand for compute failing to keep up with supply investment, which would cut AI earnings estimates and chip demand.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman expects the dollar's tailwinds to turn into headwinds only gradually next year.
tension_points.bear_case: Saravelos argues that when the equity shock is US-made, the dollar falls with stocks, since for every $1 bought there is $10 to sell.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Asian chip money stopping its flow into US stocks or flowing home, which Goldman says would remove the dollar's newest pillar.

theme_stances.key_argument: Dollar dominance now depends on US technology leadership and private sector balance sheets, which makes it inherently riskier.
theme_stances.evidence: A dollar driven by chips, AI and private capital connections should be inherently riskier.

theme_stances.key_argument: Equity flows into US AI stocks are funded by Asian chip surpluses that are themselves boosted by US AI demand.
theme_stances.evidence: There is an element of circularity to be conscious of
